Size Effect on Tensile Testing In many cases, customers may only have a limited amount of material available, which is insufficient to machine into full or sub-size tensile rods or dogbones as specified in ASTM or equivalent standards. However, it is still crucial to investigate the mechanical response of the material to ensure it can withstand the conditions it will be subjected to, particularly when modeling is not possible. This highlights the importance of exploring size effects on tensile testing. In this study, we investigated three different sizes and two distinct geometries, testing them at room temperature in accordance with ASTM E8. Ideally, a comparison with identical geometries would have been preferred, but unfortunately, this was not feasible due to the limitations of fabricating and machining full-size specimens (the largest size). Instead, we had to work with the available materials, which ultimately mimicked a real-world scenario in research, making the findings even more relevant and practical. Notably, the mechanical behavior of the specimens showed no significant difference across sizes, with yield strengths and UTS mirroring each other. The only distinction, albeit an expected one, was observed in the percentage of elongation and strain at failure, which can be attributed to the variation in specimen length. It is essential for customers to exercise caution when working with certain materials, particularly those prone to single crystals or cracking, as these defects may be captured in the gauge of the smallest specimens. Fatigue Testing Fatigue testing is often neglected in many AM studies due to funding or scope constraints, but it is crucial to determine the fatigue properties of as-built parts to emphasize the need for post- processing techniques, such as cleaning or machining, after fabrication. Rough, as-printed surfaces can serve as initiation sites for premature failure, highlighting the importance of considering surface roughness in the design and production process. It is essential to stress to the AM community that surface roughness requirements for specific applications must be clearly defined by customers and included as a processing requirement to prevent issues during use or subsequent processes to rectify roughness, which can compromise geometrical tolerances. To investigate the fatigue properties of as-built parts, a set of fatigue specimens were tested according to ASTM E606/E606M-21. The specimens were heat-treated at 650°C for 24 hours and tested in their as-printed condition. Notably, all specimens exhibited similar behavior, as shown in Figure 23, with an average total cycle to failure of 3,371.
